title: The Popular Story Behind "Let The Cat Out Of The Bag" Might Be Wrong
description:
The story behind this phrase has been repeated in etymology books for years -- but it probably never actually happened the way you've heard.

#shorts #idioms #etymology #didyouknow

scenes.text: The popular story behind "let the cat out of the bag" has been repeated in etymology books for years -- and it probably never happened the way you've heard.
The claim: dishonest market sellers would swap a live cat for a piglet inside a sealed bag, and the buyer only discovered the switch once they got home and let the cat out.
There's a problem with that story. A squirming cat feels nothing like a piglet, even through a bag -- a buyer would have noticed instantly, not later at home.
The earliest recorded use of the phrase actually comes from 1530, in a letter the reformer Johannes Agricola wrote to Martin Luther.
A second, less-repeated theory points to something else entirely: the "cat o' nine tails," a multi-tailed whip used to flog sailors, documented in print long before the phrase itself ever appeared.
Neither theory has ever been definitively proven. But etymologists generally treat the whip theory as the one with the stronger paper trail.
Which theory do you find more believable -- the market swap, or the sailor's whip?
